idiom_name: androidx.lifecycle ViewModel + StateFlow, driven by kotlinx-coroutines-test
implementation_notes: Android's documented realization: the Activity or Fragment stays a dumb view that observes state, and a ViewModel holds the screen state and the business logic, exposed as StateFlow and collected with collectAsStateWithLifecycle; kotlinx-coroutines-test drives it with runTest and injected TestDispatchers, so no device is needed. What replaces the classic humble class is the framework state holder plus dependency injection of the dispatcher; keep the ViewModel when state must survive configuration changes, and a plain state-holder class when it need not.
pitfalls: A ViewModel must not hold an Activity, Fragment, View or Context: the platform guidance warns about leaks, and such a view model cannot be constructed in a JVM unit test.
Calling Dispatchers.Main from a ViewModel makes JVM tests fail (no main dispatcher) or hang; inject the dispatcher or scope and drive the test with runTest plus advanceUntilIdle instead of sleeps.
ViewModel instances are created by the framework, so a view model with constructor parameters needs a factory (or the Compose factory) or it silently loses its dependencies.

variants.name: Compose state hoisting: stateless composable + state holder
variants.idiom_name: stateless @Composable + hoisted state holder (remember / ViewModel above the screen)
variants.implementation_notes: The declarative realization: the composable takes state and callbacks as parameters and only renders, while a state holder above the screen owns the decisions and is driven by runTest; hoist with remember (or a ViewModel) at the screen level so the logic is callable without the Composition. Choose it in Compose screens where the state need not survive process death; the ViewModel variant remains for state that must outlive the composable.
pitfalls: State created inside the composable cannot be driven from a test; hoist it above the screen or the logic has no seam.
A state holder that survives recomposition but not process death loses user state; keep ViewModel or SavedStateHandle for state that must survive both.
